summary: Eyal Blum, a Figma software engineer, frames engineering adoption of AI agents as a three-act journey: small wins with 10x speedups, painful scaling failures, then the real skill of building guardrails, prompting discipline, and context for scale. Adoption is uneven across teams that must ship together, and Figma observed several friction points: reduced developer agency and loss of craft satisfaction; the paradoxical burden on the best engineers, who hold undocumented institutional context, see pitfalls first, and become bottlenecks; and communication artifacts (docs, Slack, email) growing three to four times longer while saying roughly the same. Email volume alone has grown two to three times. Blum's prescriptive recommendations follow a verification-first philosophy: lift any check possible from humans to agent-verifiable ones (as with Playwright plus MCP), encode useful agent discoveries into deterministic repeatable flows to save tokens and time, and apply TDD-style red/green cycles so code fits the test rather than the reverse. He adapts the testing pyramid to agent review, reserving human review for functionality and pushing deterministic analysis to the base. Planning replaces prompting as the locus of craft: a week of plan-writing, peer review, and decision-flushing, then overnight implementation; good plans start with a 'why' to prevent drift, break into independently verifiable sub-PR phases (the coffee-test heuristic), and use validation gates. Skeptics should be handed the safety roadmap. Finally, communication must be attention-aware: human-typed lines at the top of PRs and messages signal where to spend scarce attention, explicitly distinguishing human from AI output. Meeting people where they already work, like tagging an agent into a Slack thread to close a loop in a non-passive-aggressive way, normalizes use and reduces friction. Blum closes by noting the journey is ongoing and that this is the biggest cultural and technological shift of his fifteen years in the valley.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Three-act adoption model and uneven team rollout
sections.summary: Blum introduces himself as a Figma software engineer and describes a three-act pattern of AI adoption: small wins, painful scaling failures, then the real skill of building guardrails and context. Adoption is uneven across teams that must ship together, and Figma has seen friction including reduced developer agency, loss of flow enjoyment, burnout, the paradoxical burden on best engineers, and bloated communication artifacts.

sections.title: Verification-first engineering and deterministic flows
sections.summary: Verification is the highest-leverage investment: lift anything possible from humans to agent-verifiable checks, as with Playwright and MCP. When an agent discovers something useful, encode it into a deterministic, repeatable flow. TDD-style red/green cycles keep agents honest by fitting code to the test rather than the reverse.

sections.title: Testing pyramid for agent review
sections.summary: Adapting the classic testing pyramid, push as much review as possible down to deterministic analysis (linting, compiler, unit tests) and reserve human review for functionality. Only leave humans to do what humans must actually be involved in.

sections.title: Planning instead of prompting
sections.summary: Planning is the replacement for the craft of writing code. A good plan starts with a 'why' to prevent agent drift, breaks into small independently verifiable sub-PR-sized phases, and uses validation gates between stages. Blum describes spending a week on a detailed plan, peer review, and decision-flushing, then sending it to an agent overnight. He notes diminishing returns to centralizing workflow choice across an org and shares an example where one week of planning replaced roughly six weeks of coding work for an approximate 5x speedup.

sections.title: Handing skeptics the roadmap
sections.summary: The skeptics are the engineers holding the codebase together with undocumented context; they see failure modes first and trust agents least. Instead of trying to convince them, give them ownership of the roadmap for making agents safe in the codebase. Their feedback is literally an ordered list of where verification is missing, and they come along once the fixes start making their own work easier.

sections.title: Attention-aware communication
sections.summary: Human attention is a scarce resource in the AI era. Blum's team has built a culture of marking what was generated by AI versus written by human so readers know how much time to spend and how much slop to expect. The PR-description convention leads with a short human-typed summary of what the code does, then places the AI description below it; reviewers pay more attention to the human top and override what they need to. The same convention applies in Slack and email: lean into the fact that everyone knows AI is being used and explicitly tell readers what to read and what to skim. The unmarked-AI-output anecdote is told in detail: a senior AI skeptic received an unmarked AI analysis of PR comments and was upset that someone they respected sent them something so sloppy; Blum apologized, recognized the need to mark AI content and intention, and treats the resulting culture change as important as the engineering work.

sections.title: Meeting people where they already work
sections.summary: Beyond fancy tools, one of the most effective adoption levers is letting people use AI where they already are. Tagging an agent into a Slack thread so it can take action and close the loop normalizes use and reduces friction. A non-passive-aggressive phrasing like 'let's see if the agent can get it this time' lets skeptics try it on their own terms; a good experience pulls them further in.

sections.title: Ongoing journey and closing
sections.summary: Blum closes by saying Figma is still learning even while shipping AI externally; the automation story is not fully there, and effective use of cloud agents is still being figured out given dependencies on internal systems. He frames the current moment as a culture and engineering shift, the biggest change by orders of magnitude he has seen in 15 years in the valley, and that everyone is figuring it out together.

demonstrations: Playwright + MCP replacing human UI navigation with agent-driven exploration.
TDD-style red/green cycles applied to agent coding so the test drives the code.
Testing pyramid adaptation: deterministic analysis (lint, compiler, unit tests) at the base, human review at the top for functionality.
Plan structure with executive summary ('why') at the top, broken into sub-PR-sized independently verifiable phases.
PR description convention: human-typed line at the top, AI-generated content below.
Tagging an agent into a Slack thread to close a loop in a non-passive-aggressive way, normalizing use for skeptics.
limitations: Blum explicitly states Figma has not come out through the other end of the adoption journey; this is mid-progress, not a finished playbook.
Centralizing one AI workflow across an organization has diminishing returns; results are highly team- and individual-specific.
Figma's automation story and effective use of cloud agents are not fully figured out yet, especially given internal system dependencies.
